newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Porsche says in talks on sport vehicle.
newsitem.headline: Porsche says in talks on sport vehicle.

text.p: Porsche AG, determined to enter the lucrative sport utility vehicle market, is holding talks with potential partners but may still opt to build the vehicle itself after breaking off talks with Mercedes-Benz AG.

Porsche chief executive Wendelin Wiedeking told Reuters in an interview at the Geneva car show on Tuesday that the vehicle would likely be introduced in 2001 or 2002 but declined to say with whom Porsche has so far held discussions.
But he said some of the talks have included potential partners in the United States, a key market for such a vehicle.

"We clearly want to go in that direction," Wiedeking said of plans to build a sport utility vehicle. "We have been looking around the world with an open mind as to where such a vehicle could be built."

Porsche had been in talks with fellow Stuttgart carmaker Mercedes to jointly produce a sport utility vehicle in the U.S. modelled on the Mercedes M class, which began production at a new factory in Alabama in January.
But the talks collapsed in January after two years of work because of concerns at Mercedes that the car would not be profitable enough.

Wiedeking said the production of a sport utility vehicle would give Porsche, which has staged a dramatic recovery after nearly facing bankruptcy in the late 1980s, a new dimension and make it less dependent on the fickle sports car market.
"The addition of a third product line through this vehicle would transform Porsche into something no one has ever seen," he said. "We will be a completely different company.
Porsche currently makes only two models, the 911 and the recently introduced Boxster roadster that has underpinned dramatic sales and profit growth at Porsche.

The dramatic demand for the Boxster prompted Porsche to sign a deal with Finland's Valmet Oy to annually build about 5,000 of the autos per year since capacity at Porsche's German factory, at 30,000 vehicles per year, has been fully exhausted.

Wiedeking said the success of the Boxster would help finance the introduction of a sport utility vehicle, which he said would be "a nightmare" for luxury carmakers who are losing potential customers to the highly-popular vehicles.
"We have the capacity and will be much more profitable in the future," he said. "We will generate enough money to finance such a project.

Wiedeking said internal studies have shown potential Porsche sport utility vehicle buyers would have a strong affinity to the vehicle and downplayed industry criticism that it was behind the curve in entering the market.
He noted that Porsche lagged BMW AG and Mercedes in entering the roadster market but said surging demand for the car was testament that Porsche had been successful.
"We have not lost time but instead we have developed a lot of competence and understand this market segment," he said.
